title: Chapter 3.  Architecture & Urban Planning — The Le Corbusier Legacy

blocks.content: This is Chandigarh's single most distinctive and heavily tested subject — no other Indian city has an entire chapter's worth of internationally significant modernist architecture and urban theory attached to it. Expect detailed questions on the sector-grid system, the '7 Vs' traffic theory, and the UNESCO-listed Capitol Complex buildings.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Chandigarh was master-planned by Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier based on the biological 'City Beautiful' concept.
The city is divided into self-contained rectangular sectors measuring 800m × 1200m, designed to provide all daily amenities within walking distance.
The '7 Vs' (Les Sept Voies) road hierarchy establishes a strict classification system ranging from regional highways to pedestrian paths.
The Capitol Complex acts as the head of the city plan, containing the High Court, Palace of Assembly, Secretariat, and the Open Hand Monument.
In 2016, the Capitol Complex was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of Le Corbusier's outstanding contribution to modern architecture.

blocks.content: Chandigarh is India's first fully planned city built after Independence, and is popularly nicknamed 'The City Beautiful'. Le Corbusier organised it as a grid of self-contained rectangular Sectors (each roughly 800 m × 1,200 m), numbered rather than named — a deliberate break from colonial-era place-naming.

Each Sector was conceived as a self-sufficient neighbourhood unit with its own shops, schools, health centre and green spaces, so that residents rarely needed to leave their own sector for daily needs — an early and influential application of the 'neighbourhood unit' principle in Indian urban planning.

Le Corbusier compared the city's overall plan to the human body: the Capitol Complex (Sector 1) as the 'head', the City Centre/Sector 17 as the 'heart', the leisure valley and green belts as the 'lungs', the industrial area as the 'hand', and the network of roads as the 'circulatory system' — this bodily metaphor is a frequently quoted, exam-favourite description.

★ EXAM POINT: Le Corbusier's body metaphor for Chandigarh — Head (Capitol Complex), Heart (Sector 17 City Centre), Lungs (Leisure Valley/green belts), Hand (Open Hand Monument/industrial area), Circulatory system (roads) — is one of the most repeated descriptive facts in Chandigarh GK.
The Capitol Complex stands as the supreme manifestation of Le Corbusier's architectural philosophy and modern urban vision.

Le Corbusier introduced a pioneering traffic-segregation system for Chandigarh — a hierarchy of seven categories of roads, each dedicated to a specific type of movement, designed to keep fast vehicular traffic separate from pedestrians and cyclists. This '7 Vs' (Sept Voies / Seven Ways) system was one of the earliest such hierarchical road classifications applied to an entire Indian city and remains a textbook example in urban planning studies.

cells: Fast regional/inter-state highways connecting Chandigarh to other cities
Arterial roads connecting sectors to each other (fast-moving through-traffic)
Sector-boundary roads encircling individual sectors (fast, but sector-peripheral)
Shopping streets within a sector (slow-moving commercial traffic)
Internal roads within a sector, connecting V4 to individual housing clusters
Access roads to individual houses within a sector
Pedestrian and cycle paths, deliberately separated from vehicular roads and often routed through green belts

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Memory aid: as the V-number increases, the road gets SLOWER and more local — V1 is a fast highway, V7 is a footpath/cycle track.

rows: Fast inter-city and regional arterial routes
Major avenues hosting key civic and commercial traffic
Fast vehicular traffic corridors surrounding each sector
Mixed vehicular and pedestrian commercial lanes inside sectors
Dedicated non-motorized greenways and walking tracks

blocks.content: The Capitol Complex (UNESCO World Heritage Site)

The Capitol Complex, located in Sector 1, is Chandigarh's most architecturally significant precinct — a cluster of monumental government buildings designed personally by Le Corbusier, executed in his signature raw-concrete 'Béton brut' style (the origin of the term 'Brutalist' architecture).

In July 2016, the Capitol Complex was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of a 17-site multinational serial nomination titled 'The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement', spanning seven countries — making it one of only a small number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India dedicated to modern (post-Independence) architecture rather than ancient or medieval heritage.

cells: Home to a court that serves BOTH states — architecturally notable for its dramatic parasol/umbrella roof providing sun protection
Seat of the joint administrative secretariat; a long horizontal block with a distinctive sun-breaker (brise-soleil) façade
Houses both states' assemblies; famous for its hyperbolic-paraboloid concrete roof and grand entrance pylon
A large rotating metal hand sculpture symbolising 'open to give, open to receive' — adopted as the official emblem of Chandigarh
Smaller symbolic/experimental structures within the Complex exploring solar-shading concepts
Commemorative structure within the Capitol Complex precinct

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Open Hand Monument is Chandigarh's official emblem, symbolising peace and reconciliation ('open to give, open to receive') — one of the most-asked one-liners in this chapter.

items: UNESCO Recognition: The Capitol Complex received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2016 under the transnational serial property of Le Corbusier's works.
Road Hierarchy (7 Vs): Questions frequently test the classification system—V1 (inter-city), V2 (city boulevards), V3 (sector-bounding fast roads), V4 (shopping streets), and V7 (pedestrian paths).
Open Hand Monument: Symbolizes the philosophy of 'open to give, open to receive' and stands 26 meters tall in the Capitol Complex.
Panjab University campus and the Chandigarh College of Architecture — designed with contributions from Pierre Jeanneret, extending the Corbusian idiom into educational buildings.
Government Museum and Art Gallery, Sector 10 — designed by Le Corbusier, houses Gandhara sculpture and miniature painting collections alongside a growing modern-art wing.

Chandigarh College of Architecture and the Pierre Jeanneret-designed furniture (notably the 'PJ Chair') produced for the city's public buildings gained major international collector value in the 2010s–2020s, with original pieces auctioned for large sums abroad — a modern trivia fact often cited to show global recognition of the city's design heritage.

Nek Chand's Rock Garden (Sector 1) stands in creative contrast to Le Corbusier's formal modernism — an entirely self-taught, informally built environmental-art space using industrial and household waste (see Chapter 7/Tourism for detail).
Chandigarh = India's first fully planned post-Independence city, nicknamed 'The City Beautiful'.
Master planner: Le Corbusier (from 1951), assisted by Pierre Jeanneret, Maxwell Fry & Jane Drew; grid of numbered Sectors, each self-contained.
Le Corbusier's body metaphor: Head=Capitol Complex, Heart=Sector 17, Lungs=Leisure Valley, Hand=Open Hand Monument, Circulatory system=roads.
'7 Vs' road hierarchy: V1 (fast highway) down to V7 (pedestrian/cycle path).
Capitol Complex (Sector 1) — UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2016, part of a 17-site global Le Corbusier serial listing across 7 countries.
Capitol Complex buildings: High Court, Civil Secretariat, Vidhan Sabha, Open Hand Monument (Chandigarh's official emblem).
Architectural style: 'Béton brut' raw concrete — origin of the term 'Brutalist' architecture.
